physical_harm: The deceased was shot dead in his clinic, resulting in homicidal death due to bullet injuries.
number_of_offences: The appellant was prosecuted for 8 offences, but only one was finally upheld.
key_evidence_accepted: The post mortem report confirming the deceased was shot from point blank range, establishing the death as homicidal.
witness_credibility: The court found the testimony of PW-14 (the sole eye-witness) to be thoroughly and wholly unreliable due to his delayed statement, lack of corroboration, and implausibility of his claim of being threatened.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed on 02.03.2013. The Supreme Court decision was on 27 August 2014.
legal_representation: P.K. Goswami, Vikas Singh for the appellant; Navnit Kumar, Corporate Law Group for the Respondent.
investigation_status: FIR registered on 3.3.1991, charge sheet filed on 29.07.2001, trial completed with conviction under Section 302 IPC.
procedural_irregularity: Non-examination of material witnesses (wife and daughter of the deceased) which affected the prosecution case.
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Section 302 IPC. High Court: Acquitted under TADA but convicted under Section 302 IPC. Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction set aside.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased was shot dead by two unidentified youths from the point blank range, and that the accused-appellant was involved in the crime. They relied on the testimony of PW-14, who claimed to be the eye-witness, and the post-mortem report indicating the cause of death was due to shock and hemorrhage from bullet injuries.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the sole witness, PW-14, was unreliable due to his delayed statement and the lack of corroboration. They also highlighted the non-examination of the deceased's wife and daughter, who were natural witnesses, and contended that the prosecution's failure to examine them created a dent in their case.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that conviction can be based on the testimony of a single witness provided he is wholly reliable, but if there are doubts about the testimony, the courts will insist on corroboration. The court also emphasized the importance of examining material witnesses and the consequences of their non-examination.
precedent_relied_upon: State of H.P. v. Gian Chand (2001) 3 SCR 247; Surinder Kumar v. State of Haryana (2011) 12 SCR 1205; Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing (2001) 6 SCC 145; Dahari v. State of U.P. (2012) 8 SCR 1219; Sunil Kumar v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) (2003) 3 SCC 169; Namdeo v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 3 SCR 939
